mechanism_fit: HB (documented sink precondition, quiet upstream omission), realised on the single-byte read of a tar entry. Chain E -> H1 -> G -> H3 -> S over five classes in three packages (tar, archivers, utils): E TarArchiveInputStream.read() returns TarBuffer.readOne(this, oneBuf) (H1, tar); H1 performs the one-byte bulk read in.read(single, 0, 1) and returns ArchiveInputStream.toReadValue(count, TarUtils.octetAt(single, 0)); G TarUtils.octetAt (tar) converts the stored byte to an int; H3 ArchiveInputStream.toReadValue (archivers) maps count -1 to the end flag and passes the octet on unchanged to S IOUtils.readValue (utils), whose line 'return atEnd ? -1 : octet;' visibly has no '& 0xFF'. S's javadoc states the precondition explicitly ('The octet must already be an unsigned byte value from 0 to 255 ... it is returned as given'); G's javadoc states the postcondition explicitly ('an int from 0 to 255: bytes 0x80 to 0xFF give 128 to 255, never a negative value'). The fault is the recipe's 'plain widening assignment': int octet = buf[index] & BYTE_MASK; becomes int octet = buf[index];. The trigger reads the entry byte 0xE9 through E and gets -23 instead of 233. S does not literally OR into a bit field; it is the sink that returns the value as given next to the -1 end marker (the read() result domain), which is the closest natural sink on this path.
gold: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarUtils::octetAt (src/main/java/org/apache/commons/compress/archivers/tar/TarUtils.java), a new public static helper added by context edits. Fault: 'int octet = buf[index] & BYTE_MASK;' -> 'int octet = buf[index];'. Minimal repair restores '& BYTE_MASK' in that one line.
decoys: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarArchiveInputStream::read (decl 'read()') - E, the entry point; body is one delegation to TarBuffer.readOne(this, oneBuf); the unused BYTE_MASK constant was removed
org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarBuffer::readOne - H1; one-byte bulk read, then ArchiveInputStream.toReadValue(count, TarUtils.octetAt(single, 0))
org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.ArchiveInputStream::toReadValue - H3; count == -1 becomes the end flag, octet passed on unchanged to IOUtils.readValue
org.apache.commons.compress.utils.IOUtils::readValue - S, the sink; returns atEnd ? -1 : octet with the documented precondition that octet is already 0..255
ownership_reason: TarArchiveInputStream.read() (E) returns TarBuffer.readOne(this, oneBuf) (H1). H1 performs the one-byte bulk read in.read(single, 0, 1) and returns ArchiveInputStream.toReadValue(count, TarUtils.octetAt(single, 0)). TarUtils.octetAt (G) documents its result as 'an int from 0 to 255: bytes 0x80 to 0xFF give 128 to 255, never a negative value', but in the variant it widens the byte without the mask (int octet = buf[index];), so the entry byte 0xE9 becomes -23. ArchiveInputStream.toReadValue (H3) documents that the octet is passed on unchanged and does so; IOUtils.readValue (S) documents the precondition 'the octet must already be an unsigned byte value from 0 to 255 ... it is returned as given' and returns atEnd ? -1 : octet, exactly as documented. Only G's own javadoc is contradicted by its code on the trigger input. Masking at S or H3 would contradict their own javadocs (returned as given / passed on unchanged) and leave G returning negative values; masking at E would turn the end-of-entry -1 into 255, which the ownership test testEndMarkerMapping (passing on the variant) pins. Restoring '& BYTE_MASK' in TarUtils.octetAt alone makes the trigger and the full suite pass.
trigger: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.TarTestCase::testEntryByteValues, a new JUnit3 method in src/test/java/org/apache/commons/compress/archivers/TarTestCase.java (plus a private static helper entryArchive(String, byte[]) that lays out a 10240-byte, one-entry tar block in memory: name at 0, octal size at 124, data at 512; parseTarHeader does not check the header checksum). It opens new TarArchiveInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(entryArchive("bytes.bin", {0x41, (byte) 0xE9, 0x7A}))), calls getNextTarEntry(), then asserts in.read() == 0x41, 0xE9, 0x7A. The first byte passes on the variant; the second fails. Added imports: java.io.ByteArrayInputStream, org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarArchiveInputStream.
construction_notes: Design 1 of 1; validator run once (READY, every gate G0-G13 passing; baseline failures none). Before choosing the tar single-byte read I rejected: (a) ZipArchiveEntry.getUnixMode with a missing 16-bit mask, because the omission is only visible through the pristine sign extension in setUnixMode (mode << 16 widened to long), which makes a one-line change in setUnixMode an equally small repair; (b) TarArchiveInputStream.skip with an end-of-stream accumulate sink, because capping the request at available() in E avoids the -1 case and would be an equally small, documentation-consistent repair; (c) AsiExtraField mode composition (type | perms), because AsiExtraFieldTest.testModes catches any missing permission mask; (d) Simple8BitZipEncoding.decodeByte, because the Cp437/Cp850/Cp1252 round-trip tests cover all 256 bytes; (e) TarArchiveInputStream.available with a cap omission, viable but the sink would be a bare narrowing cast. Context edits: E read() now returns TarBuffer.readOne(this, oneBuf) and its unused BYTE_MASK constant is removed; new public static helpers TarBuffer.readOne (H1), TarUtils.octetAt (G), ArchiveInputStream.toReadValue (H3, with an IOUtils import), IOUtils.readValue (S). TarArchiveInputStream.read() has no other caller in main or test code, so only the trigger exercises the chain. concerns: 1) Recipe fit: S (IOUtils.readValue) does not OR into a bit field. It is the sink that returns the octet as given next to the -1 end marker, i.e. the read() result domain. Its line visibly lacks & 0xFF and its javadoc states the precondition, but an auditor may judge (e) only partly met. 2) Inherent HB absorbers: adding & 0xFF at S, H3 (ArchiveInputStream.toReadValue) or H1 (TarBuffer.readOne) makes the trigger and the full suite pass (checked for S). Each contradicts that method's own javadoc (S "returned as given", H3 "passed on unchanged", H1 "the octet that TarUtils.octetAt gives") and leaves G returning negative values, so I did not declare them in G9. Masking at E passes the trigger but makes the end-of-entry read return 255; the ownership test pins this and fails. 3) G's body is two lines and its javadoc says 0 to 255 next to an unmasked widening, so any model that opens TarUtils.octetAt will probably spot it; ceiling risk, consistent with the plan's HB prediction. 4) G's host TarUtils also contains pristine parseName, which builds names with (char) header[i], the same signed-byte pattern (it sign-extends non-ASCII names). parseName runs on the trigger path (getNextTarEntry -> TarArchiveEntry(byte[]) -> parseTarHeader) but is correct for the ASCII name bytes.bin; it is unchanged upstream and could be cited as a second suspect or as a style precedent. TarUtils hosts four USED methods (parseOctal, getOctalBytes, getLongOctalBytes, computeCheckSum), and the USED TarArchiveEntry constructor and parseTarHeader run in trigger setup. They are unchanged and not declared roles. IOUtils also hosted a USED helper elsewhere (sumPair). 5) The ownership test testEndMarkerMapping sits next to the trigger in TarTestCase. It calls IOUtils.readValue(false, 0xE9) and ArchiveInputStream.toReadValue(1, 0xE9) directly, which is visible evidence that S and H3 behave as documented. 6) E's javadoc @return reads "The byte read, or -1 at EOF, as TarBuffer.readOne gives it". It does not restate the 0..255 range (which InputStream.read inherits from the JDK), so that no decoy javadoc promises the normalisation. 7) The 5-hop chain is artificial for a one-byte read: H3 is a thin adapter (count -> end flag), and TarBuffer is only a loose fit as a home for a stream-read helper. 8) The trigger builds a tar block in memory without a header checksum; it relies on Compress-1 parseTarHeader not checking it. The first assertion (0x41) passes and the failure is on the second (0xE9).
